rows.Finding description: After cholesterol supplementation from 15 to 18 DIV, somatic DQ-BSA degradation showed no significant difference between ApoE4 and ApoE3 neurons despite a lower ApoE4 trend; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: Similar to at 25 DIV, cholesterol supplementation also occasionally reduced the degradation of DQ-BSA, most often in ApoE4 neurons, although this was a nonsignificant difference (Fig. S4G).

rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE isoforms; 12.5 μg/ml cholesterol–BSA from 15 DIV for three days; somatic eight-hour DQ-BSA integrated fluorescence normalized to untreated ApoE3.

rows.Finding description: Across all cholesterol-supplemented cultures, LAMP1-associated accumulated cholesterol puncta showed no significant ApoE4–ApoE3 difference; the reported n counts embryo-derived cultures.
rows.Finding quote: I-J, quantification of number of accumulated Filipin puncta within LAMP1+ vesicles in 25 DIV neuronal cell bodies after cholesterol supplementation. Fig. J compares the differences between the group when there is an accumulation outcome (an average of four accumulated filipin puncta and higher per N). 6 to 10 fields of view per N, N (embryo) = 7 to 8, one-way ANOVA (I) p = 0.207, one-way ANOVA (J) p = 0.0005, post hoc Tukey’s E3 versus E4 p = 0.0006 (80.8% mean difference), KO versus E4 p = 0.0022 (59.3% mean difference).

rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE3 or ApoE4; 12.5 μg/ml cholesterol–BSA for three days; approximately 25 DIV neuronal somata; accumulated Filipin puncta within LAMP1 masks.

rows.Finding description: After three-day cholesterol supplementation, somatic DQ-BSA degradation showed no significant difference between ApoE4 and ApoE3 neurons; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: Even though cholesterol seemed to have an impact on endosomes, including a lower number of early endosomes (Fig. 6K), larger LAMP1+ vesicles (Fig. 6L) without altering the number (Fig. S4E), and reduced degradation of DQ-BSA after 8 h (Fig. 6M), we detected similar changes between ApoE KO, ApoE3, and ApoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4 under cholesterol loading) -> (no change in somatic DQ-BSA degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE isoforms; 12.5 μg/ml cholesterol–BSA for three days ending around 25 DIV; eight-hour DQ-BSA integrated fluorescence normalized to untreated ApoE3.

rows.Finding description: Following cholesterol supplementation in the ApoE cultures, including ApoE4, accumulated Filipin-positive droplets overlapped with LAMP1 compartments, linking lipid loading to endolysosomal storage rather than directly measuring cholesterol egress.
rows.Finding quote: Without cholesterol supplementation, Filipin dye is only seen in cell membranes. However, when supplying the cultures with cholesterol for 3 days, we could detect droplets of accumulated cholesterol that, to a large extent, overlapped with LAMP1 labeling (Figs. 6, E, F and S4B).
rows.Finding summary: (cholesterol supplementation) -> (cholesterol accumulation in LAMP1-positive compartments)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures with human ApoE targeted replacement; 12.5 μg/ml cholesterol–BSA for three days ending at approximately 25–26 DIV; Filipin and LAMP1 imaging.

rows.Finding description: Among cultures averaging at least four accumulated Filipin puncta per neuronal soma, ApoE4 had greater LAMP1-associated cholesterol accumulation than ApoE3. The joint legend gives 7–8 embryos and leaves the retained genotype-specific sample sizes unspecified.
rows.Finding quote: Thus, when only comparing cultures with detected cholesterol accumulation (cultures with an average of ≥4 Filipin accumulated droplets per neuronal cell body), there was a significant difference between ApoE4 compared to ApoE KO and ApoE3 (Fig. 6J).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4 under cholesterol loading, accumulating cultures selected) -> (greater LAMP1-associated cholesterol accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE isoforms; three-day 12.5 μg/ml cholesterol–BSA treatment ending around 25 DIV; analysis conditioned on mean ≥4 accumulated puncta per soma.

rows.Finding description: Cholesterol supplementation was described as reducing DQ-BSA degradation in cultures including ApoE4, but an ApoE4-specific treated-versus-vehicle effect size and significance test were not reported.
rows.Finding quote: Even though cholesterol seemed to have an impact on endosomes, including a lower number of early endosomes (Fig. 6K), larger LAMP1+ vesicles (Fig. 6L) without altering the number (Fig. S4E), and reduced degradation of DQ-BSA after 8 h (Fig. 6M), we detected similar changes between ApoE KO, ApoE3, and ApoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (cholesterol supplementation in APOE4 cultures) -> (lower DQ-BSA degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE4; three-day cholesterol–BSA 12.5 μg/ml treatment ending around 25 DIV; eight-hour DQ-BSA assay; plotted normalization uses untreated ApoE3.

rows.Finding description: At 18 DIV, eight-hour DQ-BSA degradation signal in neuronal somata showed no significant difference between ApoE4 and ApoE3 cultures; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: When we compared our ApoE groups at 18 DIV there were no differences in the total intensities of DQ BSA in dendrites or cell bodies between ApoE KO, ApoE3, and ApoE4 neurons after 8 h (Fig. 2, G and H).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in somatic DQ-BSA degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE3 or ApoE4; neuronal somata at 18 DIV; 25 μg/ml DQ-BSA for eight hours; background-corrected integrated fluorescence.

rows.Finding description: At 25–26 DIV, ApoE4 neuronal somata had significantly lower eight-hour DQ-BSA degradation signal than ApoE3 somata; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: Although we did not detect significant differences in LAMP1+ vesicle number and size (Fig. 4, A–E) or trafficking of EGF to the cell body (Fig. S3W) between the ApoE isoforms at 25 to 26 DIV, remarkably the degradation of DQ BSA after 8 h was reduced with ApoE4, consistent with a significant reduction in DQ BSA integrated intensity in the cell bodies compared to ApoE3 (Fig. 4, F and G, 21.9%, p = 0.0495).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower somatic lysosomal cargo degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures with human APOE targeted replacement; neurons at 25–26 DIV, designated aged; 25 μg/ml DQ-BSA for eight hours; somatic integrated fluorescence.

rows.Finding description: At 25 DIV, ApoE4 astrocytes accumulated significantly more autofluorescent granule area, used as a lysosomal lipofuscin surrogate, than ApoE3 astrocytes; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: When comparing the ApoE groups at 25 DIV, we could detect a trend toward higher levels of lipofuscin in ApoE4 compared to ApoE KO and ApoE3 neurons (Fig. 5L) and significantly higher levels of lipofuscin accumulation in ApoE4 compared to ApoE KO and ApoE3 astrocytes (Fig. 5M).

rows.Experimental system: GFAP-identified astrocytes in primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing targeted-replacement human ApoE3 or ApoE4; 25 DIV; green-channel autofluorescent-granule area.

rows.Finding description: The somatic DQ-BSA degradation response to 48-hour bicuculline stimulation showed no significant difference between ApoE4 and ApoE3 neurons; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: However, we did not detect an ApoE-dependent alteration in either endosomal morphology (Fig. S2, E–I), EGF trafficking (Fig. S2J), or DQ-BSA degradation (Fig. S2, K and L) after prolonged neuronal activity.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4 during increased excitability) -> (no change in the somatic DQ-BSA degradation response)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures with human APOE targeted replacement; 20 μM bicuculline for 48 hours from 18 DIV; eight-hour DQ-BSA fluorescence normalized to genotype-matched untreated controls.

rows.Finding description: Representative DQ-BSA images accompany the reported reduction in degradative capacity of ApoE4 versus ApoE3 neuronal somata after prolonged culture.
rows.Finding quote: Despite no apparent difference in the number and size of LAMP1+ late endosomes/lysosomes, our findings are consistent with the scenario that aged ApoE4 neurons (25–26 DIV) show lower degradative capacity that could reflect a lower number of active degradative compartments.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower somatic DQ-BSA degradation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE3 or ApoE4; neurons at 25 DIV; 25 μg/ml DQ-BSA for eight hours; fluorescence imaging.

rows.Finding description: At 25 DIV, ApoE4 neuronal somata contained significantly fewer DQ-BSA-positive compartments than ApoE3 somata; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: We further noticed that the number of vesicles containing DQ BSA in the cell bodies was significantly lower both in ApoE4 (20%, p = 0.0195) and ApoE KO (17.8%, p = 0.0048) compared to ApoE3 neurons (Fig. 4H).

rows.Finding description: At 25–26 DIV, ApoE4 neuronal somata had significantly lower total LysoTracker spot intensity than ApoE3 somata, consistent with reduced acidic-compartment labeling; n counts embryos.
rows.Finding quote: Remarkedly, similar to the DQ BSA results, we detected a 19.8% lower number of LysoTracker positive vesicles (p = 0.011) and a 35.6% lower total LysoTracker intensity per neuronal cell body (p = 0.0059) in ApoE4 compared to ApoE3 neurons (Fig. 4, I–K), supporting the scenario that ApoE4 neurons, after longer time in culture, have lower number of active degradative compartments.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower somatic LysoTracker total intensity)
rows.Experimental system: Primary embryonic mouse hippocampal/cortical mixed cultures expressing human ApoE3 or ApoE4; neuron-specific GFP labeling; 25–26 DIV; live LysoTracker imaging and Operetta spot-intensity analysis.

rows.Finding quote: Remarkedly, similar to the DQ BSA results, we detected a 19.8% lower number of LysoTracker positive vesicles (p = 0.011) and a 35.6% lower total LysoTracker intensity per neuronal cell body (p = 0.0059) in ApoE4 compared to ApoE3 neurons (Fig. 4, I–K), supporting the scenario that ApoE4 neurons, after longer time in culture, have lower number of active degradative compartments.

rows.Finding description: APOE4 mouse neurons had 23.6% less CatD-positive lysosomal area than APOE3 neurons. The Results report N = 62 neurons from six preparations for this finding without explicitly assigning that count to a genotype.
rows.Finding quote: Quantifications of the results revealed that, APOE4 neurons present a significant decrease in the areas of both the late endosomes (13% decrease, p < 0.05, N = 69 from 7 different preparations) and lysosomes (23.6% decrease, p < 0.0001, N = 62 from 6 different preparations), while no significant differences were obtained with the early and recycling endosomes (N = 65–86 from 6 to 8 different preparations).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower CatD-positive lysosomal area in mouse neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary neuronal-enriched brain cultures from 1–3-day-old human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted-replacement mouse pups on an α-syn-/- background; 2–3 pups pooled per preparation; experiments generally at culture day 21; CatD immunofluorescence and confocal quantification of labeled percentage area, without measuring cathepsin activity.

rows.Finding quote: Quantifications of the results revealed that, APOE4 neurons present a significant decrease in the areas of both the late endosomes (13% decrease, p < 0.05, N = 69 from 7 different preparations) and lysosomes (23.6% decrease, p < 0.0001, N = 62 from 6 different preparations), while no significant differences were obtained with the early and recycling endosomes (N = 65–86 from 6 to 8 different preparations).

rows.Finding description: APOE4 mouse neurons showed 35.89% lower APOER2 colocalization with lysosomes than APOE3 neurons; 25–37 cells from 2–3 preparations were reported per comparison.
rows.Finding quote: Additionally, there was also a decrease in the colocalization of the receptors with the lysosomes in APOE4 neurons that was significant in APOER2 and VEGFR but not in the IR (APOER2 : 35.89% decrease, p < 0.0001; VEGFR: 31.30% decrease, p < 0.05), and in the recycling endosomes in all three receptors (APOER2 : 11.16% decrease, p = 0.5154; IR: 30.88% decrease, p < 0.05; VEGFR: 29.02% decrease, p < 0.05) when compared to APOE3 neurons.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower APOER2 colocalization with lysosomes)
rows.Experimental system: Primary neuronal-enriched brain cultures from neonatal human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted-replacement mice on an α-syn-/- background; experiments generally at day 21; APOER2/CatD double immunofluorescence, confocal microscopy, and M1 colocalization analysis.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, one-hour recombinant apoE4 treatment increased cytosolic Cathepsin D compared with apoE3 in SH-SY5Y cells, supporting leakage from lysosomal compartments.
rows.Finding quote: Analysis of microsomal and cytosolic fractions revealed that Cathepsin D levels were increased in the cytosolic fraction of rApoE4-treated cells compared to rApoE3- and non-treated cells (Fig. 5C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher cytosolic Cathepsin D in SH-SY5Y cells)
rows.Experimental system: Human ATCC SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells treated in serum-free medium with 100 nM human recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 for 1 h; differential centrifugation to obtain microsomal and cytosolic fractions, followed by Cathepsin D immunoblotting; Ponceau staining used as loading control.

rows.Finding description: Across three experiments, recombinant apoE4 reduced Cathepsin D–Lamp-2 colocalization relative to the apoE3 condition in human primary cortical neurons, suggesting reduced lysosomal retention of Cathepsin D.
rows.Finding quote: As seen in Fig. 5E, and in agreement with the results found with SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. 5A), rApoE4-treated neurons showed reduced co-localization between Lamp-2 and Cathepsin D suggesting lower levels of Capthesin D in the lysosomes.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (reduced Cathepsin D–Lamp-2 colocalization in human primary cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Human primary cortical neurons derived from embryonic cortical tissue at 6–11 weeks post-conception, obtained after elective abortions from healthy pregnant women without known AD pathology; cultured for 10 days before treatment; 100 nM human recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 for 1 h; Cathepsin D and Lamp-2 immunocytochemistry with confocal microscopy.

rows.Finding description: Across three experiments, recombinant apoE4 produced more diffuse Lamp-2 and Cathepsin D staining and reduced their colocalization compared with apoE3 in SH-SY5Y cells, indicating impaired lysosomal retention without testing lipid-metabolism mediation.
rows.Finding quote: This pattern was not changed by treatment with rApoE3. However, treatment with rApoE4 resulted in decreased staining of both Lamp-2 and Cathepsin D with more diffuse patterns. In addition, rApoE4 exposure resulted in reduced co-localization between Cathepsin D and Lamp-2 compared to rApoE3-treated and control cells (Fig. 5A).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (more diffuse lysosomal-marker staining and reduced Cathepsin D–Lamp-2 colocalization in SH-SY5Y cells)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells obtained from ATCC; serum-free treatment with 100 nM human recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, described as lipid-free in the Discussion; Cathepsin D and Lamp-2 immunocytochemistry with confocal microscopy. Treatment duration conflicts: Results states 5 h, whereas the Fig 5A legend states 1 h.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, microsomal Cathepsin D was lower after one-hour recombinant apoE4 treatment than after apoE3 treatment in SH-SY5Y cells.
rows.Finding quote: In rApoE3 treated cells, the levels of Cathepsin D were instead increased in the microsomal fraction compared to rApoE4 treated and control cells.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower microsomal Cathepsin D in SH-SY5Y cells)
rows.Experimental system: Human ATCC SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells treated with 100 nM human recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 in serum-free medium for 1 h; microsomal fraction collected by 100,000×g centrifugation and analyzed by Cathepsin D immunoblotting; Ponceau staining used as loading control.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments after axotomy, apoE4 increased neuronal surface LRP8 while apoE3 had an intermediate effect, contrary to lower receptor surface availability with apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: In stark contrast, cultures with E4 showed increased surface LRP8 and Src activation after axotomy. The effects of E3 were intermediate.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4, after axotomy) -> (greater surface LRP8 response)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from P1 wild-type mice; day-7 axotomy; purified human apoE3 or apoE4 lipoparticles, 12 µg/ml, added 24 hours later; day-12 reelin, 2 µg/ml for 1 hour; quantitative surface-biotinylation immunoblot assay, not direct recycling-flux or binding measurements.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, axotomy left surface LRP8 unchanged without added human apoE but increased it with added apoE4, opposing the predicted loss of surface receptors.
rows.Finding quote: With no exogenous human ApoE particles added, axotomy elevated pTyr416 phospho-Src family levels moderately, but did not alter LRP8 distribution. In the presence of added E2, axotomy reduced surface LRP8 and strongly suppressed Src activation. In stark contrast, cultures with E4 showed increased surface LRP8 and Src activation after axotomy.
rows.Finding summary: (no added human apoE -> added apoE4) -> (axotomy-associated increase in surface LRP8)
rows.Experimental system: P1 wild-type mouse primary cortical neurons retaining endogenous mouse ApoE; day-7 axotomy; purified human apoE4, 12 µg/ml, added 24 hours later versus no exogenous human apoE; reelin, 2 µg/ml for 1 hour on day 12; surface-biotinylation immunoblot densitometry.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments without axotomy, added apoE4 did not substantially change surface LRP8 relative to no added human apoE, with no significant difference reported.
rows.Finding quote: Without injury, excess human ApoE did not substantially alter surface LRP8 level or Src activation (Fig. 4K, 4M and 4N).
rows.Finding summary: (no added human apoE -> added apoE4, without axotomy) -> (no change in surface LRP8)
rows.Experimental system: Uninjured primary cortical neurons from P1 wild-type mice, with endogenous mouse ApoE; purified human apoE4 lipoparticles, 12 µg/ml, versus no exogenous human apoE; reelin exposure on day 12; quantified surface-biotinylation LRP8 immunoblots.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: APOE4 addition significantly increased surface LRP1 in primary mouse neurons, providing an opposite surface-availability surrogate to impaired recycling without directly measuring recycling or binding.
rows.Finding quote: (A–C) Western blot analysis from primary neuronal culture treated with APOE (s) shows that addition of APOE4 significantly enhanced the surface LRP1 (S.LRP1) (C).
rows.Finding summary: (no added APOE4 -> added APOE4) -> (higher neuronal surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from WT P1 mouse pups; APOE4 protein at 5 μg/mL for 24 h under the supplementary Fig. 6 protocol; Pierce surface-protein biotinylation and isolation followed by Western blot quantification; three wells per condition were pooled; n units were not specified.

rows.Finding description: Quantification showed APOE4-associated elevation of neuronal surface LRP1 relative to conditioned medium alone, an opposite surface-availability surrogate to impaired recycling.
rows.Finding quote: (K–M) Western blot analysis from neuronal culture treated with ACM alone (control), APOE4+ACM, and with APOE4+GPC-4 shRNA treated ACM show that APOE4-induced surface expression of LRP1 is likely mediated through GPC-4.
rows.Finding summary: (ACM alone -> ACM plus APOE4) -> (higher neuronal surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from WT P1 mouse pups treated with WT mouse astrocyte-conditioned medium with or without APOE4; astrocytes originated from P1–2 cortices; supplementary Fig. 6 APOE protocol specifies 5 μg/mL for 24 h; surface biotinylation and isolation followed by Western blot quantification; three neuronal wells per condition were pooled.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 disruption of lipid metabolism, compared with APOE3, results in impaired late endosome/lysosome function.

rows.Finding description: TOFA treatment from embryos produced no apparent change in APOE4-associated neuronal lysosomal abnormalities relative to DMSO in young adult C. elegans (no significant difference reported, although no statistical test was supplied).
rows.Finding quote: We treated the APOE4; PVD::GFP strain with TOFA starting at the embryo stage and found that TOFA partially rescued APOE4-induced PVD neurodegeneration (Fig. 5G,H) without apparently altering APOE4-induced lysosomal defects (Fig. EV5A).
rows.Finding summary: (DMSO -> TOFA in APOE4-expressing C. elegans) -> (no change in neuronal lysosomal abnormalities)
rows.Experimental system: C. elegans expressing human APOE4 pan-neuronally through vxIs824 [rab-3p::ND18ApoE4::unc-54 3’UTR + myo-2p::mCherry::unc-54 3’UTR], with neuronal lysosomal membrane reporter ceIs56 [unc-129p::ctns-1::mCherry + nlp-21p::Venus + ttx-3p::RFP]; DMSO or TOFA treatment beginning at the embryo stage, assessed at the young adult stage by confocal fluorescence imaging. The lysosomal endpoint is reporter-defined morphology, a surrogate for function. No APOE3 comparison or direct lysosomal functional assay is reported for this result.
